name: Ulysses at the Edge
editorial_article:
"Ulysses at the Edge" is a seminal instrumental work by the American composer and instrument inventor Harry Partch. Composed in 1955 at his studio in Evanston, Illinois, the piece represents a significant transitional moment in Partch’s late-period output, marking a distinct shift away from his earlier, lyric-focused "intoning voice" works toward a more purely instrumental, percussive-driven idiom. The composition was designed to utilize his unique microtonal instrument collection, specifically featuring the Diamond Marimba and Cloud-Chamber Bowls, alongside brass elements that suggest a connection to his interest in jazz-inflected timbres—Partch reportedly originally envisioned the work for trumpeter Chet Baker.

The music of "Ulysses at the Edge" moves through dense, resonant soundscapes characteristic of Partch’s just-intonation tuning system, which allows for pure, beating-free intervals that differ significantly from the standard Western equal temperament. In the 1958 recording—which was eventually released on Gate 5 Records—Partch himself performs on the Diamond Marimba and Cloud-Chamber Bowls, accompanied by a small ensemble that includes David Reid on baritone saxophone and Dick Schleppe on alto saxophone. This ensemble-based approach highlights the textural innovation of Partch’s later career, where the physicality of the custom-built instruments defines the harmonic structure. As part of the "Ulysses" cycle, the work bridges the gap between his earlier music-dance dramas and the complex percussive explorations of his later years, remaining a crucial entry in the catalog of American 20th-century experimental music. It stands as a testament to Partch’s refusal to conform to conventional academic or classical boundaries, favoring instead a sound-world deeply rooted in ritual and raw, tactile resonance.
